subject: Mathematics
title: Aman's Swimming Pool Project
hook: A student uses quadratic equations to design a perfect swimming pool.

image.alt: Quadratic Equations: Roots and Solutions — Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Building a Home Swimming Pool
slides.storyContext: Aman's family wants to build a rectangular swimming pool with a 4-meter concrete border around it. The outer dimensions are 20m × 16m. Aman needs to find the inner pool dimensions such that the border area equals the pool area. He discovers this leads to a quadratic equation!

image.alt: Building a Home Swimming Pool — Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Quadratic Equation Definition

points.label: Standard Form
points.text: ax² + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0 (if a = 0, it's linear, not quadratic)

points.label: Degree
points.text: Always degree 2 (highest power of x is 2)

slides.inSimpleWords: A quadratic equation has x² as the highest power term.

image.alt: Quadratic Equation Definition — Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Meera Explains the Pool Problem
slides.storyContext: Meera sits with Aman and breaks down the problem: 'If the inner pool is x by y, then border area = 20×16 - xy. For balance, border area = xy. So 320 - xy = xy, which gives xy = 160. But we also need another equation! The pool's length and width shrink by 4m on each side, so x = 20-8 and y = 16-8... wait, that's fixed! Let me reframe: if both shrink by d meters, then (20-2d)(16-2d) is the pool area.'

image.alt: Meera Explains the Pool Problem — Quadratic Equations

points.label: Method
points.text: Express ax² + bx + c as (px + q)(rx + s) = 0

example.problem: Solve 2x² - 8x + 6 = 0

image.alt: Solutions by Factorization — Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Aman Tries Factorization
slides.storyContext: Aman practices with a simpler equation: x² - 5x + 6 = 0. He looks for two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to -5. He finds -2 and -3! So (x-2)(x-3) = 0, giving x = 2 or x = 3. Meera nods: 'Exactly! This works when factoring is easy. But what if the numbers don't come out so nicely?'

image.alt: Aman Tries Factorization — Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Completing the Square

points.label: Process
points.text: Convert ax² + bx + c = 0 to (x + p)² = q form

slides.inSimpleWords: Rearrange the equation so one side becomes a perfect square.

image.alt: Completing the Square — Quadratic Equations

example.problem: Solve x² + 8x + 12 = 0 by completing the square

image.alt: Completing the Square Step-by-Step — Quadratic Equations

example.problem: Solve x² + 4x - 5 = 0

image.alt: Quadratic Formula — Quadratic Equations

slides.title: The Formula to the Rescue
slides.storyContext: Meera teaches Aman the quadratic formula: 'This formula ALWAYS works, even when factoring is impossible or messy. You just substitute a, b, c and calculate. It's the universal solver for quadratic equations!'

image.alt: The Formula to the Rescue — Quadratic Equations

points.label: Discriminant
points.text: Δ = b² - 4ac

points.label: If Δ > 0
points.text: Two distinct real roots

points.label: If Δ = 0
points.text: One repeated real root (x = -b/2a)

points.label: If Δ < 0
points.text: No real roots (complex roots)

example.problem: Check nature of roots for x² - 4x + 4 = 0
example.solution: Δ = 16 - 16 = 0. One repeated root x = 2

image.alt: Nature of Roots: The Discriminant — Quadratic Equations

example.problem: For x² + 2x + 5 = 0, calculate the discriminant and tell how many real roots exist
example.solution: Δ = 4 - 20 = -16 < 0. No real roots (complex roots only).

image.alt: Check the Discriminant — Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Applications: Sum and Product of Roots

points.label: Sum of roots
points.text: α + β = -b/a

points.label: Product of roots
points.text: αβ = c/a

points.label: Use
points.text: If roots are 3 and 4, then equation is x² - 7x + 12 = 0 (since sum = 7, product = 12)

image.alt: Applications: Sum and Product of Roots — Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Aman Discovers a Shortcut
slides.storyContext: Aman learns that if he knows the sum and product of the two roots, he can write the equation immediately! Meera says: 'If roots are r and s, then equation is x² - (r+s)x + rs = 0. No need for the full quadratic formula every time!' Aman realizes he can verify his solutions using this property.

image.alt: Aman Discovers a Shortcut — Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Using Sum and Product to Build Equations

example.problem: The roots of a quadratic are 5 and -3. Write the equation.
example.solution: Sum = 5 + (-3) = 2, Product = 5 × (-3) = -15. Equation: x² - 2x - 15 = 0. Verify: (x-5)(x+3) = 0.

image.alt: Using Sum and Product to Build Equations — Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Graphical Interpretation of Roots

points.label: Parabola
points.text: y = ax² + bx + c is a parabola

points.label: Roots
points.text: Roots are x-intercepts where the parabola crosses the x-axis

points.label: Discriminant link
points.text: If Δ > 0: two crossing points; Δ = 0: one touching point (vertex on x-axis); Δ < 0: no crossing

slides.inSimpleWords: The roots are where the curve y = ax² + bx + c touches the ground (y=0).

image.alt: Graphical Interpretation of Roots — Quadratic Equations

example.problem: Inner pool dimensions: Let inner length = x, inner width = y. Border area = Pool area. Outer 20×16, border width = 4 on all sides. Setup: (20-8)(16-8) = (xy)/2... Simplified: find x if pool area = (20-2x)(16-2x) and border area = 320 - (20-2x)(16-2x). Let's use x² - 18x + 77 = 0.
example.solution: x = [18 ± √(324 - 308)] / 2 = [18 ± 4] / 2 → x = 11 or x = 7. Both valid dimensions: pool could be 11×7 meters or similar proportions.

image.alt: Swimming Pool Problem Solved — Quadratic Equations

example.problem: A ball is thrown upward with initial velocity 20 m/s. Its height at time t is h(t) = -5t² + 20t. When does it return to ground level (h = 0)?
example.solution: -5t² + 20t = 0 → t(-5t + 20) = 0 → t = 0 or t = 4. Ball returns at 4 seconds.

image.alt: Projectile Motion — Quadratic Equations

example.problem: A rectangular garden has area 120 m². The length is 7m more than width. Find length and width.
example.solution: Let width = x, length = x+7. x(x+7) = 120 → x² + 7x - 120 = 0 → (x+15)(x-8) = 0 → x = 8 (width), length = 15.

image.alt: Area and Dimensions Problem — Quadratic Equations

example.problem: A car travels x km/h. In (x-10) hours, it covers 240 km. Find its speed. Setup: x(x-10) = 240.

image.alt: Speed and Distance Problem — Quadratic Equations

example.problem: Two workers complete a job in 12 hours together. One alone takes 5 hours more than the other. Find individual times. Setup: 1/x + 1/(x+5) = 1/12.
example.solution: Simplify: 12(x+5) + 12x = x(x+5) → 12x + 60 + 12x = x² + 5x → x² - 19x - 60 = 0. Using formula or factoring: (x-20)(x+3) = 0 → x = 20. So 20 hours and 25 hours.

image.alt: Combined Work Problem — Quadratic Equations

example.problem: A quadratic y = -2x² + 8x - 3 opens downward. Find the maximum value using vertex form.

image.alt: Vertex Form and Maximum/Minimum — Quadratic Equations

slides.title: Aman Completes His Project
slides.storyContext: After weeks of studying with Meera, Aman confidently presents his pool design to Dad. Using quadratic equations, he calculated optimal inner dimensions so the border area perfectly balances with the pool area. Dad is impressed: 'This is engineering! You've used math to solve a real-world problem.' Aman realizes that every time something grows, shrinks, or relates to areas, quadratic equations might be hiding nearby.

image.alt: Aman Completes His Project — Quadratic Equations

points.text: Quadratic: ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0)
Solutions by factorization: find factors (px + q)(rx + s) = 0
Quadratic formula: x = [-b ± √(b² - 4ac)] / 2a
Discriminant Δ = b² - 4ac determines nature of roots
Sum of roots = -b/a, Product of roots = c/a
Roots are x-intercepts of parabola y = ax² + bx + c

image.alt: Key Takeaways — Quadratic Equations

example.problem: Express x = 0.333... as a fraction by solving 10x - x = 3.333... - 0.333...
example.solution: 10x - x = 3 → 9x = 3 → x = 1/3. This becomes a quadratic context in algebra.

image.alt: Recurring Decimal to Fraction Problem — Quadratic Equations

example.problem: A box with square base x and height h has volume 64 m³. If h = 64/x², cost = 3x² + 2×4xh = 3x² + 512/x. Find x minimizing cost.
example.solution: Minimize 3x² + 512/x by taking derivative or noting at minimum: 6x = 512/x² → x³ = 256/3 → x ≈ 4m.

image.alt: Optimization: Minimum Cost Problem — Quadratic Equations

subject: Mathematics
title: Sanjay's Salary Growth
hook: A young professional tracks his salary increases using arithmetic progressions.

image.alt: Arithmetic Progressions: Patterns and Sums — Arithmetic Progressions

slides.title: Annual Salary Raises
slides.storyContext: Sanjay starts his job at a tech company in Bangalore with a salary of ₹3,00,000. His manager promises a fixed raise of ₹25,000 every year. Sanjay wonders: what will be his salary in year 10? How much will he earn in total over 10 years?

image.alt: Annual Salary Raises — Arithmetic Progressions

slides.title: Arithmetic Progression (AP) Definition

points.label: Definition
points.text: A sequence where the difference between consecutive terms is constant.

points.label: Example
points.text: 3, 8, 13, 18, 23, ... (common difference d = 5)

slides.inSimpleWords: A list of numbers with constant gaps between them.

image.alt: Arithmetic Progression (AP) Definition — Arithmetic Progressions

slides.title: Sanjay Does the Math
slides.storyContext: Sanjay sits down with a calculator and starts listing his future salaries: Year 1: ₹3,00,000, Year 2: ₹3,25,000, Year 3: ₹3,50,000... He notices the pattern repeats every year. 'This looks like a sequence!' he tells Divya. Divya smiles: 'Yes, and there's a formula to predict it without writing out all 10 years.'

image.alt: Sanjay Does the Math — Arithmetic Progressions

points.label: Formula
points.text: aₙ = a + (n-1)d, where a = first term, d = common difference

example.problem: Find the 15th term of AP: 2, 5, 8, 11, ...

image.alt: General Term (nth term) Formula — Arithmetic Progressions

slides.title: Sanjay's 10th Year Salary
slides.storyContext: Using the formula, Sanjay discovers his 10th-year salary will be ₹5,25,000. He then asks Divya: 'How much will I earn TOTAL over 10 years if I don't switch jobs?' Divya says: 'That's a different question—we need to add up all 10 salaries. Let's use the sum formula.'

image.alt: Sanjay's 10th Year Salary — Arithmetic Progressions

slides.title: Sum of n Terms

points.label: Formula 2
points.text: Sₙ = n/2 × (first term + last term)

slides.inSimpleWords: Add up all terms in an arithmetic sequence using a quick formula.

image.alt: Sum of n Terms — Arithmetic Progressions

example.problem: Why does Sₙ = n/2 × (first + last)?
example.solution: Sum = a + (a+d) + (a+2d) + ... + (a+(n-1)d). Reverse: Sum = (a+(n-1)d) + ... + (a+d) + a. Add both: 2×Sum = [2a+(n-1)d] + [2a+(n-1)d] + ... (n times) = n×[2a+(n-1)d]. So Sₙ = n/2 × [2a+(n-1)d] = n/2 × (first + last).

image.alt: Sum Formula Derivation — Arithmetic Progressions

example.problem: Verify Sanjay's 10-year total: use formula Sₙ = n/2 × (2a + (n-1)d) directly.

image.alt: Calculate Total Salary Earnings — Arithmetic Progressions

slides.title: Finding Common Difference and Missing Terms

points.label: Common difference
points.text: d = aₙ₊₁ - aₙ = (second term) - (first term)

points.label: Missing terms
points.text: If AP is 3, ___, 13, then middle term = (3 + 13)/2 = 8

example.problem: Insert 3 numbers between 2 and 14 to form an AP
example.solution: We need AP: 2, a₂, a₃, a₄, 14 (5 terms total). d = (14-2)/(5-1) = 3. AP: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14

image.alt: Finding Common Difference and Missing Terms — Arithmetic Progressions

slides.title: Sanjay Checks for Odd Years
slides.storyContext: Sanjay wonders: 'What's my salary in the middle of the 10-year period?' He thinks: 'The first is ₹3,00,000 and the last (10th) is ₹5,25,000. Their average should be in the middle.' Divya confirms: 'Yes! The 5th and 6th years are in the middle. Their average is (5,00,000 + 4,75,000)/2 = 4,87,500.'

image.alt: Sanjay Checks for Odd Years — Arithmetic Progressions

points.label: Property 1
points.text: If a, b, c are in AP, then 2b = a + c (middle term is average)

points.label: Property 2
points.text: Sₙ - Sₙ₋₁ = aₙ (the nth term equals sum of n terms minus sum of (n-1) terms)

points.label: Property 3
points.text: Terms equidistant from start and end have equal sum

image.alt: Properties of AP — Arithmetic Progressions
Verify AP Property: Equal Sums — Arithmetic Progressions

He realizes that consistent growth (even modest) compounds over time. He decides to stay, understanding that mathematics helps him make smart financial decisions.

example.problem: Temperature at 6am is 15°C, increases 3°C every hour. Temp at 2pm (8 hours later)? Total sum of temps from 6am to 2pm?
example.solution: a = 15, d = 3, n = 8. a₈ = 15 + 7×3 = 36°C at 2pm. S₈ = 8/2 × (15 + 36) = 4 × 51 = 204°C (sum of all hourly temps).

subject: Mathematics
title: Ananya's Bridge Design
hook: A civil engineer uses triangle similarity to design a bridge across a river.

image.alt: Triangles: Similarity and Congruence — Triangles

slides.title: Measuring Across the River
slides.storyContext: Ananya needs to find the width of a river without crossing it. She places stakes on one bank and measures distances to a tree on the opposite bank. Using similar triangles, she can calculate the river width without actually measuring it!

image.alt: Measuring Across the River — Triangles

slides.title: Triangle Congruence Criteria

points.label: SSS
points.text: Side-Side-Side: All three sides equal

points.label: SAS
points.text: Side-Angle-Side: Two sides and included angle equal

points.label: ASA
points.text: Angle-Side-Angle: Two angles and included side equal

points.label: RHS
points.text: Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side: For right triangles

slides.inSimpleWords: Two triangles are congruent if they have the same shape and size.

image.alt: Triangle Congruence Criteria — Triangles

slides.title: Ananya's First Challenge
slides.storyContext: Vikram gives Ananya two triangles and asks: 'Are these congruent?' Ananya measures all sides of both and finds they're identical. 'Yes!' she says. Vikram nods: 'That's SSS—Side-Side-Side congruence. But what if you only knew two sides and the angle between them? That's SAS, and it still proves congruence.'

image.alt: Ananya's First Challenge — Triangles

points.label: Definition
points.text: Triangles are similar (~) if corresponding angles are equal and sides are proportional.

points.label: Notation
points.text: Triangle ABC ~ Triangle PQR means: ∠A=∠P, ∠B=∠Q, ∠C=∠R and AB/PQ = BC/QR = AC/PR

points.label: Scale factor
points.text: If AB/PQ = 2, then PQR is half the size of ABC

image.alt: Similar Triangles — Triangles

slides.title: Different Size, Same Shape
slides.storyContext: Vikram shows Ananya two triangles of different sizes but asks: 'Are they the same shape?' Ananya checks the angles—all equal! 'So they're similar, not congruent,' she says. Vikram confirms: 'Right. Similarity is about shape and proportional sides. We don't need them to be the same size.'

image.alt: Different Size, Same Shape — Triangles

slides.title: AA (Angle-Angle) Similarity

points.label: Criterion
points.text: If two angles of one triangle equal two angles of another, triangles are similar.

points.label: Why
points.text: Since angles in a triangle sum to 180°, if 2 angles match, the 3rd must also match.

points.label: Example
points.text: Triangle ABC with ∠A=60°, ∠B=70° and Triangle PQR with ∠P=60°, ∠Q=70° are similar.

slides.inSimpleWords: If two angles match, the triangles must be similar.

image.alt: AA (Angle-Angle) Similarity — Triangles

example.problem: Triangle ABC has ∠A = 50°, ∠B = 80°. Triangle DEF has ∠D = 50°, ∠E = 80°. Are they similar?
example.solution: Yes! By AA similarity. Two angles match, so the triangles must be similar. (The third angles both equal 50°.)

image.alt: Applying AA Similarity — Triangles

points.label: Theorem
points.text: If a line parallel to one side of a triangle intersects the other two sides, it divides them proportionally.

points.label: Statement
points.text: If DE ∥ BC in triangle ABC, then AD/DB = AE/EC

points.label: Use
points.text: Finding unknown segment lengths

example.problem: In triangle ABC, DE ∥ BC. If AD = 4, DB = 6, AE = 5, find EC

image.alt: Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT) — Triangles

slides.title: Ananya Learns the Parallel Line Trick
slides.storyContext: Vikram explains: 'If you draw a line parallel to the base of a triangle, it creates a smaller similar triangle inside. And the sides are divided proportionally!' Ananya draws it: 'So if I know some lengths, I can find others without measuring everything?'

image.alt: Ananya Learns the Parallel Line Trick — Triangles

slides.title: Similar Triangles in Real Life: River Crossing

points.label: Setup
points.text: Ananya places a stake at point A on one bank and measures AB = 100m along the bank to point B.

points.label: Measurement
points.text: At A, she faces the tree T on the opposite bank. She walks perpendicular 6m to point C, then finds the point D where C, T, and another stake align.

points.label: Calculation
points.text: Triangle ABC ~ Triangle D'TC' (by AA similarity). If CD = 4m, river width AT = (AB × CD) / AC

slides.inSimpleWords: Use similar triangle ratios to find unknown distances.

image.alt: Similar Triangles in Real Life: River Crossing — Triangles

points.label: Theorem
points.text: In a right triangle, a² + b² = c² (where c is hypotenuse)

points.label: Converse
points.text: If a² + b² = c², then the triangle is right-angled.

example.problem: A ladder 13m long leans against a wall. Base is 5m from wall. How high does it reach?

image.alt: Pythagoras Theorem in Triangles — Triangles

slides.title: Pythagoras Saves Time
slides.storyContext: Ananya must find the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 7m and 24m. Instead of measuring, she uses Pythagoras: c² = 49 + 576 = 625, so c = 25m. Vikram smiles: 'That's a famous triple—7, 24, 25. Pythagoras works every time for right triangles.'

image.alt: Pythagoras Saves Time — Triangles

example.problem: Right triangle has hypotenuse 26m and one leg 10m. Find the other leg.
example.solution: a² + 10² = 26² → a² + 100 = 676 → a² = 576 → a = 24m. So the legs are 10m and 24m.

image.alt: Finding Missing Side with Pythagoras — Triangles

example.problem: Ananya stands at point A. She marks a line AB = 100m along the bank. At A, she sights a tree T across the river. From point B, the angle ABT = 30° and angle TAB = 90° (she stands perpendicular to river). Using similar triangles, find AT (river width).
example.solution: In triangle ABT: angle TAB = 90°, AB = 100m. In similar triangle formed by her measurements, if she measures a proportional distance: tan(30°) = AT/AB → AT = 100 × tan(30°) = 100/√3 ≈ 57.7m

image.alt: Ananya's River Width Problem (Solved) — Triangles

example.problem: A vertical pole casts a shadow of 12m when the sun is at 45° elevation. A nearby tree casts a shadow of 18m at the same time. Find the tree's height.
example.solution: Pole height/shadow = tan(45°) = 1 → Pole height = 12m. Tree and pole triangles are similar: Tree height / 18 = 12/12 = 1 → Tree height = 18m.

image.alt: Shadow Problem — Triangles

example.problem: A bridge support forms two right triangles. Left: legs 8m and 15m. Right: legs 16m and x. If the triangles are similar, find x.
example.solution: Similar right triangles: 8/16 = 15/x → x = (15×16)/8 = 30m. Scale factor is 2:1.

image.alt: Bridge Foundation Problem — Triangles

slides.title: Ratio of Sides in Similar Triangles

example.problem: Triangle ABC ~ Triangle PQR with scale factor 2:3. If AB = 8m, find PQ.
example.solution: Scale factor 2:3 means Triangle ABC is 2/3 the size of PQR. So 8/PQ = 2/3 → PQ = 12m.

image.alt: Ratio of Sides in Similar Triangles — Triangles

example.problem: Triangle ABC is isosceles with AB = AC = 10cm and base BC = 12cm. Triangle PQR has PQ = PR = 15cm and base QR = 18cm. Are they congruent or similar?
example.solution: AB/PQ = 10/15 = 2/3, BC/QR = 12/18 = 2/3. All ratios equal, so ABC ~ PQR (similar, not congruent). Scale factor 2:3.

image.alt: Isosceles Triangles and Congruence — Triangles

slides.title: Ananya Completes the Bridge Design
slides.storyContext: After months of applying triangle similarity, AA criteria, and Pythagoras theorem, Ananya presents the bridge design to Vikram. 'I calculated the river width using similar triangles, verified all angles match across the foundation supports, and ensured the support beams satisfy the Pythagoras relation for diagonal strength.' Vikram nods approvingly: 'Mathematics keeps people safe.'

image.alt: Ananya Completes the Bridge Design — Triangles

points.text: Congruent triangles: same shape AND size (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS)
Similar triangles: same shape, different size (AA criterion)
BPT: parallel line divides sides proportionally
Pythagoras: a² + b² = c² in right triangles
Scale factor shows how much one triangle is enlarged/reduced
Applications: surveying, shadows, bridge design, architecture

image.alt: Key Takeaways — Triangles

example.problem: Triangle ABC ~ Triangle PQR with scale factor 2:3. If area of ABC is 40 cm², find area of PQR.
example.solution: Area ratio = (scale factor)² = (2/3)² = 4/9. Area of PQR = 40 × (3/2)² = 40 × 9/4 = 90 cm².

image.alt: Area of Similar Triangles — Triangles

example.problem: Triangle ABC: sides 6, 8, 10 cm. Triangle PQR: sides 9, 12, 15 cm. Are they similar?
example.solution: Check ratios: 6/9 = 2/3, 8/12 = 2/3, 10/15 = 2/3. All equal! ABC ~ PQR by SSS similarity. Scale factor 2:3.

image.alt: SSS Similarity Criterion — Triangles

example.problem: In right triangle ABC with right angle at C, altitude from C to hypotenuse AB divides it into segments 9 and 16. Find AC and BC.
example.solution: In right triangles, altitude h satisfies: AC² = 9×(9+16) = 9×25 = 225 → AC = 15. BC² = 16×25 = 400 → BC = 20. Verify: 15² + 20² = 225 + 400 = 625 = 25².

image.alt: Altitude in Right Triangle — Triangles

example.problem: Equilateral triangle has side 10 cm. Find altitude and area using Pythagoras.
example.solution: Altitude h: h² + 5² = 10² → h² = 75 → h = 5√3 cm. Area = (1/2) × 10 × 5√3 = 25√3 cm².

image.alt: Equilateral Triangle Properties — Triangles

example.problem: In triangle ABC, the three medians meet at centroid G. If median from A has length 12 cm, AG divides it in ratio 2:1. Find AG and GM.
example.solution: Centroid divides each median in 2:1 from vertex. AG = (2/3)×12 = 8 cm, GM = (1/3)×12 = 4 cm.

image.alt: Medians and Centroids — Triangles
